analysis.one_liner: Strengthens black lung benefits for coal miners with easier claims, higher payments, and stricter coal company insurance rules.
analysis.headline: The bill to fix the black lung claims process and raise miner benefits never received a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it easier for coal miners sickened by black lung disease to win disability benefits: government-paid medical evaluations, an automatic approval when scans show the advanced form of the disease, government-paid lawyer fees, and reopened claims that were denied using x-ray readings from doctors the Labor Department later discredited. It would also raise the benefit to $9,627.60 a year starting in 2024 and tie future increases to inflation, and would require coal companies that self-insure to prove they can actually pay, with penalties rising from $1,000 to $25,000. It was introduced in November 2023 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with black lung disease and their surviving spouses and dependents. Miners with the advanced form of the disease (complicated pneumoconiosis or progressive massive fibrosis) would win benefits automatically without having to prove total disability in adversarial litigation. Claimants would get government-funded pulmonary evaluations and CT scans, attorneys would be paid up to $4,500 in fees plus $3,000 in medical expenses from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund so miners who cannot afford a lawyer can get one, and miners whose earlier claims were denied based on x-rays read by doctors later discredited by the Labor Department could have those cases reopened with back pay. All beneficiaries would see their monthly checks rise to $9,627.60 per year and keep pace with inflation going forward.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners and surviving family members

how_it_helps.text: Creates an irrebuttable presumption of total disability for any miner whose x-ray, CT scan, biopsy, or autopsy shows complicated pneumoconiosis or progressive massive fibrosis, taking the advanced, most disabling cases out of adversarial litigation entirely.

Requires the Labor Secretary to provide claimants a complete pulmonary evaluation at government expense, authorizes CT scans when x-rays show pneumoconiosis, and bars doctors who work for or were retained by the coal company opposing the claim from performing the evaluation, with a published, conflict-screened list of qualified physicians.

Establishes a program paying attorneys' fees (up to $4,500) and unreimbursed medical expenses (up to $3,000) in contested claims that drag past two years, addressing the problem the bill's findings cite: only 42 percent of claimants have a lawyer at the initial claims stage, while coal companies have far greater legal and medical resources.

Raises the benefit to $9,627.60 per year beginning in 2024 and indexes it to the Consumer Price Index, ending a system where benefits were frozen whenever federal employees' pay was frozen, and lets miners whose claims were denied using x-ray readings from discredited physicians file new claims with back pay to the original denial.

Requires coal operators to meet financial-health criteria to self-insure their black lung liabilities, raises the penalty for failing to secure payment from $1,000 to $25,000, extends personal liability to CEOs, COOs, and other responsible parties, and makes companies that go bankrupt owe the Trust Fund the difference between the value of benefits it must pay and any security recovered.

Makes knowingly false statements, witness intimidation, and attorney misconduct in black lung proceedings punishable by up to 5 years' imprisonment and permanent disqualification from black lung cases, and requires judges to sanction parties that refuse to comply with discovery orders.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators. Companies that self-insure would have to meet financial-health tests and post security covering current and projected liabilities, face penalties of up to $25,000 with personal liability reaching their executives, and reimburse the Trust Fund, with interest, for medical evaluations and attorney fees whenever a claim results in an award. The Black Lung Disability Trust Fund — financed by a coal excise tax — would initially front the cost of medical evaluations and attorney fees, and would bear the cost of the benefit increase where no solvent operator can be held liable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and the Trust Fund

drawbacks.text: The benefit increase, attorney fee program, and government-funded medical evaluations all draw on the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which the bill's own findings describe as the overextended backstop when self-insured companies default; the operator-reimbursement provisions only recoup costs when a claim actually wins and a solvent operator is found, so the Trust Fund's deficit could deepen in the interim.

Extending personal liability for unpaid benefit obligations to chief executives, chief operating officers, and any business under common control with an operator, plus a 25-fold penalty increase, imposes new compliance and legal exposure on coal companies — a cost smaller operators would feel hardest, which some would argue could pressure margins in an already declining industry.

The automatic-benefit presumption for the advanced form of the disease and the sanctions regime for attorneys and experts on either side change a decades-old adversarial claims process quickly; the bill directs the Secretary to write implementing rules within 12 to 18 months, and administrative transition would fall on an Office of Administrative Law Judges already facing a backlog the bill instructs it to reduce to under 12 months per case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to a specific, heavily burdened group — miners with an often-fatal occupational disease and their families — while its costs fall mostly on the coal companies whose dust caused the disease, which Congress's findings say was the original intent. The main honest cost concern is the Trust Fund: the bill front-loads new spending (fees, evaluations, higher benefits) onto a fund already strained by decades of company defaults, and recoups those costs only case-by-case from liable operators. The financial-security provisions in Section 131 are designed to fix that over time, but the fund would carry the risk in the meantime. On balance the design is coherent — strengthen the claims process and shore up the fund's solvency in the same bill — but its fiscal footing depends on rules the Secretary had yet to write.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health and labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey introduced the Black Lung Benefits Improvement Act of 2023 on November 15, 2023, joined by five Democratic colleagues including both Pennsylvania senators, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, and West Virginia's Joe Manchin.

The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — and no further action of any kind followed: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.

The bill was a comprehensive rewrite of the black lung claims process, based on findings that only 42 percent of claimants have an attorney at the initial stage, that benefits failed to keep pace with inflation during federal pay freezes, and that company defaults pushed costs onto the public Trust Fund.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee with none of its provisions enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off: they avoid stricter self-insurance requirements, a $25,000 penalty, personal executive liability, and a claims process tilted toward miners. Miners with pending claims gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal mine operators avoiding new costs

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its findings on the resource imbalance between coal companies and miners.

for.name: Sen. John Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill the day it was introduced.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both coal-state and other Democratic senators.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 15, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote; the bill died there.

against.name: The full Senate
against.what_they_did: Never debated or voted on the bill at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, including coal-state senators Manchin and Fetterman, but no vote was ever taken in committee or on the floor, so the partisan shape of opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill targets the industry's two biggest advantages in black lung claims: its superior legal and medical resources, and its practice of self-insuring without real collateral and defaulting onto the public Trust Fund. Operators would face conflict-screened government medical evaluations, an automatic benefit for the most advanced cases, penalties rising from $1,000 to $25,000, personal liability for executives, and mandatory reimbursement with interest.

industries.industry: Physicians and consulting firms providing defense x-ray readings (B-readers) for coal companies
industries.note: Doctors employed by, contracted to, or recently retained by the party opposing a claim could no longer perform the government's pulmonary evaluations, and any physician or expert witness who makes false statements would be permanently disqualified from black lung cases. Claims previously denied on readings from doctors the Secretary discredited could be reopened.

industries.industry: Black Lung Disability Trust Fund (financed by the coal excise tax)
industries.note: The bill draws on the fund to pay attorney fees, medical evaluations, and higher benefits, but also shores up the fund by requiring financially sound self-insurance and making defaulting companies and their executives liable for the full actuarial value of benefits the fund must cover.
